modules.title: Module 1: Introduction To Economics as a Science

sections.title: 1.1 . Basic Concepts: Wants, Scarcity, choice, scale of preference, opportunity cost, Rationality, production, distribution, consumption.
sections.content:
Economics is a social science that studies how human beings allocate scarce resources to satisfy unlimited wants. 

According to Lionel Robbins (1932), "Economics is the science which studies human behavior as a relationship between ends and scarce means which have alternative uses."It is classified as a social science because it applies scientific methods (observation, hypothesis, data collection, and laws) to study dynamic human behavior under the assumption of Ceteris Paribus (all other things being equal).

Core Economic Concepts

Wants: The unlimited, competitive, and recurring desires of human beings for goods and services (e.g., wanting a phone, mobile data, or new clothes).

Scarcity: The fundamental economic problem where resources are permanently limited relative to infinite human wants.

Choice: Selecting specific wants out of many due to limited resources and income.

Scale of Preference: A list of an individual's unsatisfied wants arranged in order of priority or relative importance. It helps allocate limited income efficiently to maximize satisfaction.

Opportunity Cost (Real Cost): The next best alternative forgone when a choice is made. It is the physical item sacrificed (e.g., foregoing a pair of shoes to buy a textbook), NOT the money spent.

JAMB Exam Focus: Lionel Robbins' definition is the standard tested in UTME. Remember: Opportunity cost is always the item forgone, never the money spent or the item purchased!

Basic Economic Activities

Production: The creation of utility to satisfy human wants. It is complete only when goods reach the final consumer.

Primary production: Extractive activities (e.g., farming, crude oil drilling).

Secondary production: Manufacturing and processing (e.g., turning cassava into garri, refining crude oil).

Tertiary production: Commercial and personal services (e.g., banking, transport, teaching).

Distribution: Moving goods from producers to final consumers through channel middlemen:
$$\text{Producer} \longrightarrow \text{Wholesaler} \longrightarrow \text{Retailer} \longrightarrow \text{Consumer}$$
